result: TRUST is a novel imaging system that uses UV-LED illumination and a color camera to achieve simultaneous widefield exogenous fluorescence and endogenous autofluorescence imaging with block-face serial sectioning, eliminating the need for tissue clearing or extensive sample preparation.
evaluation: Claims C1, C34-C36, C40, C47-C48, C136-C137 collectively describe the core technical approach of TRUST. The system design is well-documented with detailed descriptions of the optical setup (C47-C48, C177-C178), the use of UV surface excitation for shallow penetration depth (C35, C47), and the integration with vibratome sectioning (C36). The manuscript provides extensive experimental validation across multiple organ types demonstrating the capability.

result: TRUST employs real-time staining with fluorogenic dyes (DAPI and PI) during imaging, which takes approximately 150 seconds per layer and provides advantages over traditional pre-staining methods in terms of time efficiency and staining uniformity.
evaluation: Claims C2, C37-C38, C56, C58-C59, C61-C63, C74, C79, C193 describe the real-time staining approach. The manuscript provides quantitative data on staining time (~150s, C56, C193) with supporting figures (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), explains the theoretical basis for time savings based on diffusion kinetics (C37), and demonstrates uniform staining throughout whole-organ imaging (C74, C77). The use of fluorogenic probes with >20-fold fluorescence enhancement (C62) is well-supported by citations.

result: TRUST successfully imaged a complete mouse brain and all vital organs (heart, liver, kidney, lung, spleen) from adult mice, generating high-quality 3D reconstructions with subcellular resolution without image registration.
evaluation: Claims C3, C44, C66-C73, C93, C138 describe the experimental validation of TRUST on multiple organs. The manuscript provides detailed quantitative data for each organ including imaging volumes, voxel counts, section numbers, and acquisition times (C71, C73, C94, C96, C102, C107, C109). Multiple figures (Figures 2-3) show high-quality images of anatomical structures. The claim of registration-free 3D reconstruction (C72) is supported by the stable sectioning performance demonstrated in the results.

result: TRUST demonstrated capability for developmental biology by imaging whole mouse embryos at E15 and E18, with complete E15 embryo imaging achieved in approximately 2 days.
evaluation: Claims C4, C45, C115-C116, C118, C123-C125, C139 describe embryo imaging results. The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on imaging times (~2 days for E15 whole embryo, C4, C124; ~3 days for E18, C125) and volumes. Multiple figures (Figure 4) show detailed anatomical structures and developmental comparisons. The imaging quality is validated by comparison with histological images (C122) and consistency with known developmental biology (C120-C121, C129-C130).

result: Double labeling with DAPI and PI provides superior imaging contrast and biological information compared to single-dye staining, with PI revealing neuronal cytomorphology while DAPI labels nuclei, enabling differentiation of cell types and providing Nissl-like contrast.
evaluation: Claims C42, C80-C84 describe the advantages of double labeling. The manuscript provides comparative data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing improved image quality with double labeling versus PI alone (C80). The differential staining properties are supported by citations (C81 cites Hezel et al., 2012) and demonstrated in multiple figures showing clear differentiation of brain structures (C83, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

result: TRUST utilizes endogenous autofluorescence to identify anatomical structures including axons, nerve tracts, myelinated fiber bundles, and blood vessels without exogenous labeling, with multicolor imaging enabling extraction of different tissue components from different color channels.
evaluation: Claims C85-C92 describe autofluorescence imaging capabilities. The manuscript provides extensive visual evidence (Figure 2g-k, w-x) showing identification of multiple structures based on autofluorescence. The use of different color channels to separate tissue components (C89-C91) is demonstrated with supporting figures (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). The extraction of 3D structures (C92) is shown in Figure 2t-v with described image processing methods.

result: Comparison of E15 and E18 embryo images reveals developmental changes consistent with known embryology, including appearance of the inner plexiform layer in retina, differentiation of brain ventricular zones, ossification of cartilage, submandibular gland lumenization, and changes in cell nuclear size due to differentiation.
evaluation: Claims C120-C121, C128-C135 describe developmental observations. Each claim is supported by specific figures (Figure 4e, k, l, p-r, v-x; Figure 5a-e) and validated by citations to prior work (Fan et al., 2016; Savolainen et al., 2009; Larsen et al., 2010; Graham et al., 2015; Yi et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2017). The consistency with histological images (C122, C130, C133) and known developmental timelines (C129, C132) provides strong validation.

result: TRUST has anisotropic resolution with lateral resolution of ~1.25 μm but axial resolution of 10-50 μm, limited by vibratome sectioning thickness and UV optical sectioning depth.
evaluation: Claims C141-C145 describe resolution limitations. The lateral resolution measurement (C142) is supported by quantitative data with a figure (Figure 1—figure supplement 6). The axial resolution limitation (C143) is acknowledged with citations to other techniques for comparison. The causes are clearly identified (C144) and the practical sectioning thickness used (50 μm for most samples, 10 μm demonstrated for liver, C145) is documented throughout the results.

result: TRUST provides an outstanding balance of time-efficiency, imaging resolution, and cost-effectiveness compared to other 3D imaging systems, making it particularly suitable for large sample imaging and developmental biology studies.
evaluation: Claims C78, C136-C139 summarize the overall advantages of TRUST. The manuscript provides comparative data (Supplementary file 1b referenced in C78) and demonstrates the claimed advantages through extensive experimental validation across multiple organs and embryos (C138-C139). The elimination of sample preparation steps (C136) and use of inexpensive components (UV-LED, color camera) support the cost-effectiveness claim.

result: Resolution can be improved using higher NA objective lenses with deconvolution algorithms (e.g., Lucy-Richardson) or deep-learning-based super-resolution networks to recover resolution when using lower magnification objectives.
evaluation: Claims C150 and C158 describe resolution improvement methods. Both are supported by figures showing the results (Figure 1—figure supplement 7 for deconvolution, Figure 1—figure supplement 8 for deep learning). The deconvolution approach shows ~2× improvement in both lateral and axial resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 7f1-f2). These are demonstrated capabilities, not just speculation.

result: Traditional mechanical sectioning and staining methods are labor-intensive, require complex image registration, and can induce uncorrectable distortions due to slice ruptures.
evaluation: Claims C5-C8 describe limitations of traditional methods. These are well-established facts in the field, supported by appropriate citations (Amunts et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2015; Ju et al., 2006). The claims provide context for the development of TRUST and are based on established knowledge and cited literature.

result: Tissue clearing combined with light-sheet fluorescence microscopy has achieved impressive results for whole-brain imaging, but faces challenges including limited resolution due to long working distance objectives, time-consuming clearing processes, and potential tissue degradation.
evaluation: Claims C9-C20 describe the state of tissue clearing and LSFM. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015; Huisken et al., 2004; Matsumoto et al., 2019; Murakami et al., 2018; and others). These provide accurate context for the field and are based on established knowledge with proper attribution.

result: Block-face serial sectioning tomography offers advantages for large specimen imaging including no need for tissue clearing and easy scalability, but faces challenges of high cost, time-consuming processing, and slow imaging with point-scanning systems.
evaluation: Claims C21-C30 describe block-face serial sectioning approaches. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior work describing various implementations (Seiriki et al., 2017, 2019; Economo et al., 2016; Ragan et al., 2012; and others). These accurately represent the state of the field and provide context for TRUST development.

result: Wide-field large-volume tomography (WVT) proposed real-time labeling to reduce staining time, but requires resin embedding that causes tissue shrinkage due to dehydration.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33 describe WVT and its limitations. All claims are supported by appropriate citations (Gong et al., 2016; Rodgers et al., 2021; Gong et al., 2013). These provide accurate context for how TRUST improves upon WVT by eliminating the need for resin embedding.

result: TRUST can use alternative fluorogenic dyes including Nile red and DiI for lipid staining, which are nearly nonfluorescent in polar solvents but show fluorescence enhancement in nonpolar environments.
evaluation: Claims C43, C166, C194-C195 describe lipid staining capabilities. The manuscript provides visual evidence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing successful imaging with these dyes. The properties of the dyes (C194) are based on established knowledge, and compatibility testing (C195) is documented.

result: In liver tissue, TRUST can differentiate hepatocytes and anatomical structures including portal vein, sinusoids, and focal inflammation, with vessel network extraction possible through image processing, and finer 10 μm sectioning enables better resolution of microstructures like sinusoids.
evaluation: Claims C97-C101 describe liver imaging capabilities. Visual evidence is provided in multiple figures (Figure 3h-i for structures, Figure 3j for vessel network, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 for fine sectioning). The image processing workflow is documented (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and the advantage of finer sectioning (C101) is a logical inference supported by the demonstrated results.

result: In kidney tissue, veins and glomeruli can be clearly recognized, with all glomeruli extracted using the Detectron2 machine learning library trained on manually labeled TRUST images.
evaluation: Claims C103-C104 describe kidney imaging and analysis. Visual evidence is provided (Figure 3m-n for structures, Figure 3o for extracted glomeruli). The use of Detectron2 (C104) is documented with citation (Wu et al., 2019) and the training approach (two sections manually labeled) is described in the methods.

result: Lung tissue sectioning is challenging due to porous structures, but filling with 10% gelatin through the trachea followed by post-fixation enables successful imaging of anatomical structures including artery, bronchiole, and alveolus.
evaluation: Claims C105-C108 describe lung tissue preparation and imaging. The problem is documented with visual evidence (Figure 3—figure supplement 5a-b), the solution is described in detail (C106), and successful results are shown (Figure 3p-s). The imaging time and volume data (C107) are provided, and anatomical structures are clearly identified (C108).

result: In spleen tissue, white pulp and red pulp can be clearly differentiated with typical structures like germinal center and marginal zone visible, and white pulp regions can be extracted from the blue channel using simple thresholding.
evaluation: Claims C110-C111 describe spleen imaging and analysis. Visual evidence is provided (Figure 3x-y for structures, Figure 3v for extracted white pulp). The image processing approach (simple thresholding based on blue appearance, C111) is straightforward and supported by the visual results.

result: Multiple potential improvements to TRUST are proposed including better vibratomes, UV-absorbing dyes, fresh tissue imaging, additional fluorogenic probes, automated immunostaining, spectral filtering, and optimized staining protocols, though most require future development.
evaluation: Claims C146, C148-C149, C160-C176, C199-C200 describe potential future improvements. While some preliminary results are shown (C161 for fresh tissue), most of these are speculative proposals for future work rather than demonstrated capabilities. The manuscript appropriately frames these as future directions, but they cannot be considered supported results of the current work.

result: The TRUST system uses specific optical components including a UV-LED (M285L5), objective lens (Plan N 10×/0.25 NA), tube lens, aluminum mirror, color camera (DS-Fi3), and a vibratome (VF-700-0Z) with automation controlled by an Arduino-based MCU and LabVIEW interface.
evaluation: Claims C177-C182 describe the technical implementation details. All components are specifically identified with model numbers and manufacturers. The system design is documented in figures (Figure 1a-c) and the automation system is described in detail. These are straightforward technical specifications of the implemented system.

result: Sample preparation involves harvesting organs from sacrificed mice, rinsing with PBS, fixing in 10% NBF for 24 hours, and embedding in agarose or gelatin with tissue-specific protocols, with all procedures approved under license AEP16212921.
evaluation: Claims C183-C189 describe sample preparation protocols. The methods are clearly documented with specific concentrations, times, and conditions. Tissue-specific variations are noted (C185-C188) with appropriate citations. Ethical approval is documented (C189). These are standard protocols appropriately described.

result: Image processing includes automated conversion of binary files to TIFF, real-time stitching without registration based on stage positions, flat-field correction, linear blending, and optional notch filtering, with manual masking for background removal.
evaluation: Claims C201-C210 describe image processing methods. The workflow is documented with appropriate citations for standard methods (Seibert et al., 1998; Solina and Leonardis, 1999). The rationale for registration-free stitching (C205-C206) is explained based on high-precision stages and flat sectioning. These are standard image processing approaches appropriately applied.

result: 3D structures can be extracted from TRUST images based on color or intensity characteristics, with specific features appearing in different color channels (nerve fibers in blue/green, nuclei in red, white pulp in blue/green, vessels as negative contrast), and rendered with pseudo color for visualization.
evaluation: Claims C211-C221 describe image analysis and rendering methods. The extraction methods are documented with visual evidence in multiple figures. The use of Detectron2 for glomeruli (C211) is cited. The rendering approach using Amira or ImageJ (C212) is standard. The color characteristics of different structures (C215-C218) are demonstrated in the figures.

result: Agents like Triton X-100 used to increase tissue permeability can increase sample transparency by removing lipids, which deteriorates TRUST imaging contrast due to increased UV light penetration depth.
evaluation: Claims C75-C76 describe a limitation of using permeabilization agents with TRUST. The effect is documented with visual evidence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b-g). This is a logical consequence of the UV surface excitation principle - increased transparency defeats the shallow penetration depth that enables optical sectioning.

result: The field of view in TRUST is relatively small (600 μm × 450 μm) with the current camera (chip size: 6.91 mm × 4.92 mm) and 10× objective lens.
evaluation: Claim C156 provides a quantitative specification of the FOV. This is a straightforward technical specification that can be calculated from the camera chip size and objective magnification. The manuscript acknowledges this as a limitation and discusses potential solutions.
